newsitem.title: USA: US lawmakers seek penalties for copyright breaches.
newsitem.headline: US lawmakers seek penalties for copyright breaches.

text.p: U.S. lawmakers introduced a bill on Friday to impose criminal penalties on people who violate copyright laws but do not profit from the violations.

"Under current copyright law, it is illegal to willfully infringe on any amount of copyrighted material if done for profit or material gain," Rep. Chris Cannon, Republican of Utah, said. "There is no criminal penalty attached in the absence of a profit motive."

If the bill is enacted into law, violators could be prosecuted simply for electronically distributing copyrighted material worth a total of at least $5,000. "Stealing is stealing, regardless of value or personal gain," Cannon said.

The legislation is meant to close a loophole that allowed a Massachusetts Institute of Technology student in 1994 to beat copyright violation charges after he posted on the Internet for free downloading copies of popular commercial software like Wordperfect and Microsoft Excel. Prosecutors contended Internet users downloaded over $1 million worth of the pirated software.

The court said the actions of the student, David LaMacchia, were "heedlessly irresponsible" and "lacking in any fundamental sense of values." But since LaMacchia did not profit from the violations, the court dismissed the copyright charges.

The bill, called the No Electronic Theft Act, was authored by Virginia Republican Bob Goodlatte and is also sponsored by Massachusetts Democrat Barney Frank and North Carolina Republican Howard Coble.

Sottware companies strongly supported the bill. "Quick passage of this bill is critical to providing an important deterrent in curbing software piracy," Robert Holleyman, president of the Business Software Alliance, said.
But Internet law specialist Paul Terry of Winthrop, Stimson, Putnam & Roberts said the $5,000 amount might be too low given how easily software can be copied and downloaded on the Internet.
"It is an admirable goal that they're trying to achieve but the drafting threshold seems pretty low," Terry said.
The Senate is considering a similiar bill written by Vermont Democrat Pat Leahy.

Leahy's bill would criminalize making 10 or more copies with a total value of at least $5,000. The bill imposes misdemeanor penalties if the value is less than $10,000 and up to three years in prison if the value exceeds $10,000.

The bill would also expand the definition of "financial gain" to include bartering. People who pirate software on the Internet often trade and barter the illegally copied works, referred to as "warez."
